opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Joe. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won't be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, for sure. Is this going to take long? Just asking, it's all good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the chatbot's kind of annoying, but whatever. People still want to see the apartment with a real person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the bot already does most of what I used to do. I mostly do tours now and chase late paperwork. If it stays like this I'm fine, I guess, but I don't really know what I'm for anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep showing up. Try to be the one people ask for on tours, so my manager sees I'm useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of weird. Like waiting to get called into the office.

S0.say: The chatbot's annoying, but people still want a real person to show them the apartment.
S0.think: The bot already does most of his old job. He mostly gives tours now and isn't sure what he's for.
S0.do: Keeps turning up and tries to be the one people ask for on tours.
S0.feel: Kind of weird, like waiting to get called into the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm lucky I already got in, because they're not hiring guys like me anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm the beginner they won't hire, except I'm already here. So I'm probably first to go when they cut. I'm not the best at the paperwork side, everyone knows that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe ask my manager what I should learn. Maybe the real estate licence, if it's not too hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe the licence. Is that something you'd really start this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? Probably not unless someone pushes me. I'm bad at studying. But I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. Not freaking out yet.

S1.say: I'm lucky I already got in, because they're not hiring guys like me anymore.
S1.think: He's the kind of beginner they've stopped hiring and knows he's weak on paperwork, so he'd go first.
S1.do: Thinks about asking his manager what to learn and maybe a real estate licence, though he admits he probably won't start without a push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's messed up. They replace people with bots and the rent still goes up every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's gone. Like, that's it. The bot does enquiries, the app does the lease, they'd just need someone to unlock doors, and there's a smart lock for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start looking at other jobs straight away. Warehouse, delivery, a restaurant, anything. Maybe move back home if I can't make rent with my roommates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I don't really have a plan.

S2.say: It's messed up. They replace people with bots and the rent still goes up every year.
S2.think: His job is gone. The bot does enquiries, the app does leases and a smart lock opens doors.
S2.do: Starts looking for warehouse, delivery or restaurant work and thinks about moving back home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who own the buildings get richer and people like me get nothing. It's not fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At least, like, physical jobs are still there in this one. I could do warehouse or kitchen work. It pays bad but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a warehouse job or a kitchen job. Keep living with roommates. Maybe borrow from my mom if it gets bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad, but I can still see a way through.

S3.say: Building owners get richer and people like me get nothing. It's not fair.
S3.think: At least physical jobs are still there. Warehouse or kitchen work pays badly but it's something.
S3.do: Gets a warehouse or kitchen job, keeps sharing with roommates and may borrow from his mom.
S3.feel: Bad, but he can still see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something angry. Like, where are we supposed to work now?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That was my backup. Warehouse, kitchen. If robots take those too, I have nothing. No degree, no savings, no skill they'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Move back with my mom, for sure. Maybe the army. I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to pick one thing to do first, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Call my mom. Then probably sign up for whatever the government gives out, if they give anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like there's no floor. Like I'm falling.

S4.say: Where are we supposed to work now?
S4.think: Warehouse and kitchen work were his backup. Without them he has no degree, no savings and no skill anyone wants.
S4.do: Moves back with his mom, signs up for any government help and thinks about the army.
S4.feel: Like there's no floor and he's falling.
